inline.s: [Vyakarana] The Buddha names in advance (records the name): after how many ages, in such and such a place, in such and such a land, one will become what Buddha.

[Thus know: to walk a thousand miles, the first step must be right; if the first step is wrong, the whole thousand miles are wrong. To enter the land of the unconditioned, the initial faith must be right; once the initial faith is lost, all good retreats. Therefore the patriarch said: “A hairsbreadth’s deviation, and heaven and earth are set apart.” This is the principle.]

Therefore know: to walk a thousand miles, the first step must be right; if the first step is wrong, then all the thousand miles that follow are wholly wrong. To enter the land of the unconditioned (the true mind), the initial faith must be right (one must believe that one is originally a Buddha); if the initial faith is lost and not right, then all good retreats. Therefore the patriarch said: “A hairsbreadth’s deviation, and heaven and earth are set apart.” This is the principle.
[The unconditioned] That which is made by no causes or conditions. [The land of the unconditioned] Another name for the true mind (see the next chapter, “The True Mind’s Other Names”).

[Someone says: I have already given rise to right faith, but I do not know what is named the true mind. The answer: Apart from delusion it is called true; numinous awareness is called mind. The Surangama Sutra sets forth and reveals this mind.]

Someone asks: I have already given rise to right faith, but I do not know what is called the true mind. The answer: Apart from delusion it is called true; numinous knowing is called mind. The Surangama Sutra sets forth and reveals this mind.

[Someone says: It is only called the true mind; has it yet other different names? The answer: In the teachings of the Buddhas and the teachings of the patriarchs the names established are not the same. And in the Buddhist teachings: the Bodhisattva Precepts Sutra calls it the mind-ground, because it gives rise to all good; the Prajnaparamita Sutra names it bodhi, because it takes enlightenment as its essence; the Avatamsaka Sutra establishes it as the dharma-realm, because it interpenetrates and contains all; the Diamond Sutra names it the Tathagata, because it comes from nowhere; the Prajnaparamita Sutra calls it nirvana, because it is the refuge of all sages; the Golden Light Sutra names it suchness, because it is true and eternally unchanging; the Vimalakirti Sutra names it the dharma-body, because the reward-body and transformation-body rely on it; the Awakening of Faith names it true suchness, because it neither arises nor ceases; the Nirvana Sutra calls it the Buddha-nature, because it is the essence of the three bodies; the Perfect Enlightenment names it the all-holding dharani, because it pours forth merit; the Srimala Sutra names it the tathagata-garbha, because it hides, covers, and contains all; the Sutra of Definitive Meaning names it perfect enlightenment, because it shatters darkness and shines alone. Therefore the Chan Master Shou, in the Verses on Mind Only, says: “One dharma, a thousand names; names are set up in accord with conditions.” They are complete in the many sutras, and cannot all be quoted.]

Someone asks: You have explained what the true mind is; has the true mind yet other names? The answer: The teachings and the Chan lineage give the true mind different names. In the teachings, the Bodhisattva Precepts Sutra calls it the mind-ground, because it gives rise to all good; the Prajnaparamita Sutra names it bodhi, because it takes enlightenment as its essence; the Avatamsaka Sutra establishes it as the dharma-realm, because it interpenetrates and contains all; the Diamond Sutra names it the Tathagata, because it comes from nowhere; the Prajnaparamita Sutra calls it nirvana, because it is the refuge of all sages; the Golden Light Sutra names it suchness, because it is true and eternally unchanging; the Vimalakirti Sutra names it the dharma-body, because the reward-body and transformation-body rely on it; the Awakening of Faith names it true suchness, because it neither arises nor ceases; the Nirvana Sutra calls it the Buddha-nature, because it is the essence of the three bodies; the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment names it the all-holding dharani, because it pours forth merit; the Srimala Sutra names it the tathagata-garbha, because it hides, covers, and contains all; the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment again names it perfect enlightenment, because it shatters darkness and shines alone. Therefore the Great Master Yongming, in the Verses on Mind Only, says: “One dharma has a thousand names; names are set up in accord with conditions.” The many names of the true mind in the teachings are all in the many sutras, and cannot one by one be fully quoted.

[Bodhisattva Precepts Sutra] Kumarajiva of the Yao Qin dynasty finally translated the tenth chapter, the Bodhisattva Mind-Ground Precepts, of the Brahma Net Sutra, in two fascicles, entitled “The Brahma Net Sutra, Chapter Ten: The Bodhisattva Mind-Ground Precepts Spoken by Vairocana Buddha.” Later, the precepts spoken after the verses in the lower fascicle were extracted separately as one fascicle, for the convenience of recitation and upholding; the Tiantai master Zhiyi named it the Bodhisattva Precepts Sutra. [Prajnaparamita Sutra] The general name for the scriptures that set forth the profound and wondrous doctrine of prajnaparamita.

[Someone says: The Buddhist teachings are already known; what of the patriarchs’ teaching? The answer: Under the patriarchs’ gate, names and words are cut off; since no name is established, how could there be many more names? Yet in response to the stimulus of capacities, its names are likewise many.]

Someone asks: The many names of the true mind in the teachings are already known; then what names does the Chan lineage have? The answer: Under the patriarchs’ gate, names and words are cut off; since even a name is not established, how could there be many more names? Yet in response to the stimulus of capacities, the true mind has quite a few names.

[Sometimes it is called the self, because it is the nature of sentient beings; sometimes it is named the right eye, because it beholds all characteristics; sometimes it is named the wondrous mind, because it is empty and numinous, still and illuminating; sometimes it is named the master, because it has borne the burden from the first; sometimes it is called the bottomless bowl, because it makes its living wherever it is; sometimes it is called the stringless lute, because its melody comes forth in the present; sometimes it is named the inexhaustible lamp, because it shatters the deluded mind; sometimes it is named the rootless tree, because its root and stem are firm; sometimes it is called the sword of the hair-splitter, because it cuts off the roots of dust; sometimes it is named the land of the unconditioned, because the seas are calm and the rivers clear; sometimes it is named the Mani pearl, because it relieves the poor; sometimes it is named the boltiess lock, because it shuts the six senses; and further it is named the mud ox, the wooden horse, the mind-source, the mind-seal, the mind-mirror, the mind-moon, the mind-pearl.]

Sometimes it is called the self, because it is the nature of sentient beings; sometimes it is named the right eye, because it beholds all characteristics; sometimes it is named the wondrous mind, because it is empty and numinous, still and illuminating; sometimes it is named the master, because from the first it is the one that acts; sometimes it is called the bottomless bowl, because it lodges its living wherever it is; sometimes it is called the stringless lute, because its melody comes forth in the present; sometimes it is named the inexhaustible lamp, because it shatters the deluded mind; sometimes it is named the rootless tree, because its root and stem are firm; sometimes it is called the sword of the hair-splitter, because it cuts off the roots of dust; sometimes it is called the land of the unconditioned, because the seas are calm and the rivers clear; sometimes it is named the Mani pearl, because it relieves the poor; sometimes it is named the boltiess lock (a lock without a spring), because it shuts the six senses; and further it is named the mud ox, the wooden horse, the mind-source, the mind-seal, the mind-mirror, the mind-moon, the mind-pearl, and so on.
[The seas are calm and the rivers clear] The great sea has no waves, the Yellow River is clear. [Mani pearl] That is, the mani jewel, also named the wish-fulfilling pearl. [The spring of the “lock” (
xu
)] The reed-spring in a lock.

[These various different names cannot all be recorded. If one penetrates the true mind, all the names are understood; if one is benighted about this true mind, all the names become obstructions. Therefore, as to the true mind, one should be most careful.]

The various other names of the true mind cannot one by one be enumerated. If one penetrates the true mind, then as to all the names of the true mind one will understand that they are speaking of the true mind; if one is benighted about this true mind, then as to all the names of the true mind one will feel them obstructive, not knowing whether they speak of something else. Therefore, as to the various names of the true mind, one must judge by the context and discern them most carefully.

Here it must be explained that this one essence with different names, this one essence with many names appearing in the sutras and treatises, is for the sake of breaking students’ attachment to names and characteristics; the ancient Chan gate likewise customarily used this device of “one dharma, a thousand names; names set up in accord with conditions.” Yet one essence with many names is hard for modern people, educated from childhood in science, to accept. Some even reproach and challenge it on this account, holding it to be wrong, unscientific, and logically confused. For in science there is an unwritten rule: if a book or a paper is to use a technical term, it must first give a clear definition (except for terms familiar in textbooks), and from beginning to end it uses only that one term; if there is an exception, it must be noted. Therefore, when we study the sutras and treatises and meet this one essence with different names, one essence with many names, and even cases that cross and overlap, we should know that this is not the ancients’ logical confusion; they had their own intent. We ourselves must judge by the context what this or that name actually refers to, and accomplish “if one penetrates the true mind, all the names are understood,” so as to avoid misunderstanding.

blocks.text: 3. The Wondrous Essence of the True Mind

inline.s: [Someone says: The true mind’s name is already known; what of its essence? The answer: The Prajnaparamita Sutra of the Light-Emitting says: “Prajna has no characteristic of any kind, no characteristic of arising or ceasing.” The Awakening of Faith says: “The essence of true suchness itself: in all ordinary men, hearers, solitary realizers, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas, there is no increase or decrease. It is not born in the former limit, nor does it cease at the latter limit; ultimately it is eternal. From the very beginning its nature has of itself fulfilled all merit.”]

Someone asks: I already know the various names of the true mind; what then is the essence of the true mind? The answer: The Prajnaparamita Sutra of the Light-Emitting says: “Prajna has no characteristic of any kind, no characteristic of arising or ceasing.” The Awakening of Faith says: “The essence of true suchness itself: all ordinary men, hearers, solitary realizers, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas have no increase or decrease. It is not born in the former limit, nor does it cease at the latter limit; ultimately it is eternal. From the very beginning, the essence of the true mind of itself (by its own nature) fulfills all merit.”
[The former limit and the latter limit] The past is named the former limit; the future is named the latter limit.

[According to these sutras and treatises, the essence of the true mind transcends cause and effect, runs through past and present, establishes neither ordinary being nor sage, and has no opposites of any kind. Like great empty space it pervades all places; its wondrous essence is still and silent. It cuts off all idle discourse; it neither arises nor ceases, is neither existent nor nonexistent, neither moves nor shakes, and is clear and permanently abiding. It is called the master of former days, named the man on the far shore of Awesome Sound, and also named the self before the empty kalpa. With one equal mind, without the least flaw or film, all mountains, rivers, and the great earth, grasses, trees, and thickets, the myriad appearances in dense array, and all dharmas pure and defiled all come forth from within it.]

According to these sutras and treatises, the essence of the true mind transcends cause and effect, runs through past and present, establishes neither ordinary being nor sage, and has no opposites of any kind (no mutual opposition of this and that). Like great empty space it pervades all places; its wondrous essence is still and silent. It cuts off all idle discourse; it neither arises nor ceases, is neither existent nor nonexistent, neither moves nor shakes, and is clear and permanently abiding. It is called the master of former days, named the man on the far shore of Awesome Sound, and also named the self before the empty kalpa. With one equal mind (regarding all things equally), without the least flaw or film, all mountains, rivers, and the great earth, grasses, trees, and thickets, the myriad appearances in dense array, and all dharmas pure and defiled all come forth from within it.

[Idle discourse] Words that contain a playfulness and are unreal. [The far shore of Awesome Sound] Before the Buddha Awesome Sound King, or again before the appearance in the world of the Buddha Awesome Sound King. The Buddha Awesome Sound King is a Buddha who appeared in an extremely remote past age; the Chan groves borrowed this Buddha’s name to indicate a time in the past that is extremely remote. “The far shore (
pan)

] means that side. “The far shore of Awesome Sound” is a phrase the Chan groves commonly used to point students to their own original face, the same in meaning as “before one’s parents were born.” [The empty kalpa] One of the four kalpas, that is, after this world has been destroyed, during which there is only empty space. [The four kalpas] In one great kalpa there are the four intermediate kalpas of the kalpa of formation, the kalpa of dwelling, the kalpa of destruction, and the kalpa of emptiness, and each intermediate kalpa in turn has twenty small kalpas. What is called “formation” is the world being composed by the gathering of many conditions; “dwelling” is sentient beings abiding at rest, with plants and animals, with lands and borders, with history; “destruction” is the beginning of ruin: in the first nineteen small kalpas all plants and animals are destroyed, and in the last small kalpa the lands and worlds on which sentient beings rely are destroyed; “emptiness” is that when the destruction is complete, all alike become empty space. Thus the world unceasingly goes through formation, dwelling, destruction, and emptiness, cycling around without end. [Equal mind] An equal mind, without love and hate, taking and rejecting.

[Therefore the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Good son, the supreme Dharma King has a great dharani gate named perfect enlightenment. From it flow forth all purity, true suchness, bodhi, nirvana, and the paramitas, teaching bodhisattvas.” Guifeng says: “As for the mind, it is empty and wondrous, subtle and pure, brightly luminous and numinously clear; it neither goes nor comes, and secretly penetrates the three times; it is neither middle nor outside, and thoroughly illumines the ten directions. It neither ceases nor arises: how could the four mountains harm it? It is apart from nature and apart from characteristics: how could the five colors blind it?” Therefore Yongming, in the Verses on Mind Only, says: “As for this mind, all wonders and all spirits universally assemble in it, and it is the king of all dharmas; the three vehicles and the five natures secretly return to it, and it is the mother of a thousand sages. Alone honored, alone noble, without peer or equal, it is truly the source of the great Way, the essential truth of the Dharma.”]

Therefore the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Good son, the Tathagata (the supreme Dharma King) has a great all-holding Dharma gate named perfect enlightenment. It ceaselessly flows forth purity, true suchness, bodhi, nirvana, and the paramitas, to teach bodhisattvas.” The Great Master Guifeng says: “As for the mind, it is empty and wondrous, subtle and pure, brightly luminous and numinously clear; it neither goes nor comes, and secretly penetrates the three times; it is neither middle nor outside, and thoroughly illumines the ten directions. It neither ceases nor arises: how could the four mountains (birth, old age, sickness, and death) harm it? It is apart from nature and apart from characteristics: how could the five colors (blue, yellow, red, white, and black) blind it?” Therefore the Great Master Yongming, in the Verses on Mind Only, says: “As for this mind, all wonders and all spirits universally assemble in it, and it is the king of all dharmas; the three vehicles and the five natures secretly return to it, and it is the mother of a thousand sages. Alone honored, alone noble, without peer or equal, it is truly the source of the great Way, the essential truth of the Dharma.”

[Empty and wondrous] Serene and still. [Brightly luminous] Bright and radiant. [The three times] Also named the three ages, that is, past, present, and future. [The four mountains] A simile for the four marks of birth, old age, sickness, and death. It means that birth, old age, sickness, and death have nowhere to be escaped, like four mountains closing in together. The Nirvana Sutra says: “There are four great mountains that come from the four directions, wishing to harm the people. The four great mountains are birth, old age, sickness, and death.” [The three vehicles] The vehicle of the hearers, the vehicle of the solitary realizers, and the vehicle of the bodhisattvas. [The five natures] The Faxiang school divided the faculties of all sentient beings into five kinds, called the five natures. First, those who have the undefiled seed by which the fruit of arhatship can be cultivated are named the definite nature of the hearers. Second, those who have the undefiled seed by which the fruit of the pratyekabuddha can be cultivated are named the definite nature of the solitary realizers. Third, those who have the undefiled seed by which the fruit of Buddhahood can be cultivated are named the definite nature of the bodhisattvas. Fourth, those who have two or three of the above kinds of undefiled seed, so that the stage they will realize in the future depends on conditions ripening and is not fixed as to which fruit they will realize, are named the indefinite nature. Fifth, those who do not have the undefiled seed of the above three vehicles but have the defiled seed by which the fruit of gods or men can be cultivated are named the natureless. [Without peer (
chou
)] There is none that can be compared with it.

[Believe it, and the bodhisattvas of the three times study together, for they study this mind; the Buddhas of the three times realize together, for they realize this mind; the whole canon of one treasury sets forth and reveals, for it reveals this mind; all sentient beings are deluded and confused, for they are deluded about this mind; all practitioners awaken, for they awaken to this mind; all the patriarchs transmit to one another, for they transmit this mind; the monks of the world under heaven call and visit, for they call and seek this mind.]

Believe as said above, and what the bodhisattvas of the three times study together is the study of this mind; what the Buddhas of the three times realize together is the realization of this mind; what the whole canon of one treasury sets forth and reveals is the revelation of this mind; all sentient beings are deluded and confused, for they are deluded about this mind; all practitioners awaken, for they awaken to this mind; all the patriarchs transmit to one another, for they transmit this mind; the monks of the world under heaven call and visit, for they call and seek this mind.
[For] A classical Chinese particle that introduces a statement.

[Penetrate this mind, and everywhere is the Way, and every thing fully manifests it; be deluded about this mind, and everywhere is inversion, and every thought is foolish madness. This essence is the Buddha-nature inherent in all sentient beings; it is the root-source from which all worlds arise and develop. Therefore the World-Honored One was long silent on Vulture Peak, and Good Manifestation beneath the cliff forgot
(in ancient usage the same as “to die,” that is, to be silent)

words, Bodhidharma gazed at the wall at Shaoshi, and the layman held his tongue at Vaishali: all of them revealed the wondrous essence of this mind. Therefore one who has just entered the patriarchs’ gate must first recognize the essence of this mind.]

Penetrate this mind, and everywhere is the Way, and every thing fully manifests the wondrous principle; be deluded about this mind, and everywhere is inversion, and every thought is foolish and mad delusion. The essence of this mind is the Buddha-nature inherent in all sentient beings; it is the root-source from which all worlds arise and develop. Therefore the World-Honored One was long silent at the assembly on Vulture Peak, Subhuti sat in silence beneath the cliff, the patriarch Bodhidharma gazed at the wall at Shaolin Monastery, and the layman Vimalakirti held his tongue in the city of Vaishali: all of them used the wordless word to reveal the wondrous essence of this mind. Therefore one who has just entered the patriarchs’ gate must first recognize the essence of this mind.

[Everywhere is the Way] The state after awakening: mind and realm merge, inside and outside become one piece, and even eating and dressing, carrying water and gathering firewood, every movement and every act, every opening of the mouth and every closing of it, is a single matter undarkly merged with the “wondrous Way.” As is said, “Everywhere is the Way; every dharma is originally perfect.” [Vulture Peak] Gridhrakuta, Vulture Mountain, abbreviated Spirit Mountain, also translated as Mount Jijue; the mountain is named because its shape resembles a vulture and vultures were numerous on it. It lies northeast of Rajagriha, the capital of Magadha in Central India, and is the place where Shakyamuni Buddha taught the Dharma. [The World-Honored One was long silent on Vulture Peak] At the Lotus assembly on Vulture Peak (Gridhrakuta) the World-Honored One was long silent before revealing the meaning of the sutra; three times before this he only said: “Stop, stop; it need not be spoken. My Dharma is wondrous and hard to conceive.”]

[Good Manifestation] The translated name of Subhuti. [Good Manifestation forgot words beneath the cliff] Subhuti sat in silence (in still meditation) among the rocks, and the gods rained flowers in praise. The elder said: “You rain flowers in the sky and praise me; who then are you?” The answer: “I am Brahma.” The elder said: “What do you praise?” Brahma said: “I honor the venerable one for well expounding prajnaparamita.” The elder said: “I have never spoken a single word of prajna; what do you praise?” Brahma said: “The venerable one did not speak, and I did not hear. Not speaking and not hearing: this is truly expounding prajnaparamita.” And again the earth shook and flowers rained down. [Shaoshi] A separate peak of Mount Song. Emperor Xiaowen of Wei built the Shaolin Monastery there for the Chan Master Buddha, and it is the place where the First Patriarch Bodhidharma sat facing the wall for nine years. [Vaishali] The city of Vaishali, the dwelling place of the layman Vimalakirti. [The layman held his tongue at Vaishali] Vimalakirti once questioned the assembled bodhisattvas on the Dharma gate of non-duality, and they in succession set forth the meaning of non-duality in words; at the last Manjushri questioned Vimalakirti, and Vimalakirti held his tongue and silently did not answer, and Manjushri then sighed in admiration. For the Dharma gate of non-duality is beyond the reach of words and explanations, and so Vimalakirti’s single silence surpassed the words of all the bodhisattvas.
There was of old the koan of “Xiangyan strikes the bamboo”:

the Chan Master Xiangyan Zhixian was a man of Qingzhou. Weary of the vulgar he left his kin, and traveled the regions seeking the Way. In the time of Baizhang his nature and understanding were sharp and quick, yet he could not penetrate Chan. When
ji,
that is, when he had reached and come to
Baizhang passed into transformation
when he had come to the Chan Master Baizhang’s parinirvana

he went to study under Guishan. Guishan asked: “I have heard that in the place of your late master Baizhang you answered ten when asked one and answered a hundred when asked ten; this is your cleverness and sharp wit. Understanding and interpretation, consciousness and thought
this is

are the root of birth and death. Before your parents were born, try and say one phrase.” At this one question the master was utterly at a loss. He returned to his quarters and took up the texts he had read in former days, meaning to search from the beginning for a single phrase to answer with, yet in the end he could not find one. Then he sighed to himself: “A painted cake cannot fill the belly.” Again and again he begged Guishan to explain it to him. Guishan said: “If I explained it to you
if I were to explain it for you

you would curse me hereafter. What I say is mine, and in the end has nothing to do with you.” The master then burned all the texts he had read in former days, saying: “In this life I will not study the Buddha Dharma. I will be a long-traveling monk of gruel and rice, and spare my mind its labor.
He wept and took leave of Guishan. He went straight through to Nanyang, and seeing the traces of the National Teacher Zhong
the National Teacher Huizhong
he rested there. One day, as he was cutting
shan,
cutting grass
he happened to fling away a piece of tile, which struck a bamboo and made a sound, and he was suddenly awakened. Quickly
ju,
urgent

he returned, bathed, and burned incense, and from afar bowed in homage to Guishan, praising him: “The master’s great compassion exceeds that of my parents. Had he then explained it to me, how would there have been today’s matter?” And he had a verse, saying: “One strike, and knowing is forgotten; no more is cultivation needed. In every movement the ancient path is exalted
every movement manifests the ancient path of the sages: seeing the nature and becoming a Buddha
not falling into the trap of quiet stillness
not emptily guarding dead quietude
Everywhere without traces
the wondrous essence of the true mind
beyond sound and form its dignity
the dignity of the wondrous essence of the true mind surpasses sound and form
Those who have reached the Way in every quarter all speak of
all say
the supreme capacity.” When Guishan heard it, he said to Yangshan: “This one is thoroughly
greatly awakened

). Yangshan said: “This is the mind’s mechanism and consciousness, accomplished by writing. Wait until I myself have personally tested him.” Later Yangshan saw the master and said: “The master praises the junior brother for revealing the great matter. Try and say something.” The master recited his former verse. Yangshan said: “That was accomplished by memorizing former habits. If you have a true awakening, say something else.” The master made another verse: “Last year poor, it was not yet poverty; this year poor, then it is poverty. Last year poor, I still had ground to plant a needle (to stand a needle: ten thousand thoughts return to one); this year poor, there is not even a needle (there is not even ground to stand a needle: the one thought returns to nothing).” Yangshan said: “The Tathagata Chan, we grant, the junior brother understands. The patriarchs’ Chan, he has not dreamed of it.” The master had yet another verse: “I have one mechanism; a blink of the eye (a blink, the time of a blink) regards it (him). If a man does not understand, then (turning away) call him a novice monk.” Yangshan then reported to Guishan: “I am glad to say the junior brother Xian (Zhixian) understands the patriarchs’ Chan.” (from the Wudeng Yantong)

[Tathagata Chan] The Chan methods prevalent in the eastern land before Bodhidharma came from the west, such as breath-counting Chan, the five-gate Chan, and so on. Their characteristic is: relying on the teachings to cultivate contemplation, gathering the mind into concentration, and advocating liberation through meditative concentration.

[Patriarchs’ Chan] The Chan method transmitted by the patriarch Bodhidharma: not establishing words, a special transmission outside the teachings, pointing directly at the human mind, seeing the nature and becoming a Buddha. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “It speaks only of seeing the nature; it does not discuss meditative concentration and liberation.” [A special transmission outside the teachings] The Chan school sets up no writings and establishes no words and phrases, but directly transmits the Buddha’s and the patriarchs’ mind-seal, which is called “a special transmission outside the teachings,” meaning a special transmission apart from the Tathagata’s verbal teachings. The Sutra of the Great Brahma King Asking the Buddha to Resolve Doubts says that the Brahma King came to Spirit Mountain and offered the Buddha a golden lotus flower, requesting the Buddha to speak the Dharma. The World-Honored One twirled the flower before the assembly and did not speak the Dharma, and for a time the millions of gods and men all failed to understand his meaning; only the Elder Kashyapa broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said: “I have the treasury of the correct Dharma eye, the wondrous mind of nirvana, the mark of reality that is no-mark, the subtle and wondrous Dharma gate, which is not established in words and is a special transmission outside the teachings. I entrust it to Mahakashyapa.” This is the origin of the Chan school. Therefore the patriarchs’ Chan also originates from the Tathagata; it is only a special transmission outside the teachings. [The treasury of the correct Dharma eye] The Buddha’s mind-eye thoroughly beholds the correct Dharma, and is named the “correct Dharma eye”; being deep and wide and containing ten thousand virtues, it is called the “treasury.”

[I have one mechanism] The five aggregates of body and mind are constantly compared to a mechanical wooden man (a wooden figure driven by a mechanism). The “mechanism” in the phrase “I have one mechanism” is a simile for the mechanism (the self-nature) that drives the wooden man (the five aggregates of body and mind). The Treatise on the Perfection of Great Wisdom says: “There is no maker at all. Is this matter an illusion? Is it a mechanical wooden man, or a matter in a dream?” The Surangama Sutra says: “Though one sees the faculties moving, they must be drawn by one mechanism; when the mechanism is stilled and returns to silence, all illusions become without nature.” [A blink of the eye regards it] This is precisely the state the Fifth Patriarch Hongren spoke of in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch: “one who has seen the nature must see it at the word (as soon as it is spoken, he sees)”; and so Yangshan certified that Xiangyan understood the patriarchs’ Chan. [At the word] Beneath a single word; instantly. [Call him a novice monk] When the master (Yangshan) was a novice monk, a monk asked Shishuang: “What is the meaning of the patriarch’s coming from the west?” Shishuang said: “If a man in a well a thousand feet deep can get out without using an inch of rope, that man will answer you the meaning of the coming from the west.” The monk said: “Recently the monk Chang of Hunan has appeared in the world and likewise speaks east and west for people.” Shishuang called the novice monk: “Drag out this corpse.” The master afterwards asked Danyuan: “How can the man in the well get out?” Danyuan said: “Ha! Fool! Who is in the well?” The master went and asked Guishan. Guishan called: “Huiji (Yangshan’s name)!” The master responded. Guishan said: “He is out!” After the master had settled, he often brought up these former words and told the assembly: “I got my name at Danyuan’s place, and got my ground at Guishan’s place.” (From the Sayings of the Chan Master Huiji of Yangshan in Yuanzhou.)

[What is the meaning of the patriarch’s coming from the west?] The First Patriarch of Chan, Bodhidharma, came from the western heaven to this land to transmit the Dharma: what is its essential purport?

blocks.text: 4. The Wondrous Function of the True Mind

inline.s: [Someone says: The wondrous essence is already known; what is called its wondrous function? The answer: The ancients said: “When the wind moves, the mind shakes like a tree; when clouds arise, the nature stirs up dust. If one understands today’s matter, one is benighted as to the original man.” This is the wondrous function arising from the wondrous essence.]

Someone asks: The wondrous essence of the true mind is already known; what then is the wondrous function of the true mind? The answer: The ancients said: “When the wind of conditions moves, the mind shakes like a tree; when the clouds of obstruction arise, the nature stirs up dust like dust; if one takes the things around one as real and is turned by them, one loses the original man.” This is the wondrous function arising from the wondrous essence of the true mind.

This passage says that even what is done in delusion is the wondrous essence of the true mind at work, only that it is the perverse function of the true mind when deluded. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“The self-nature can contain the ten thousand dharmas, and is named the storehouse consciousness. If thinking arises, that is the turning consciousness, which produces the six consciousnesses, goes out through the six gates, and sees the six dusts; thus the eighteen realms all arise as functions of the self-nature. If the self-nature is perverse, it gives rise to eighteen perverse functions; if the self-nature is right, it gives rise to eighteen right functions. If the function is evil, it is the function of sentient beings; if the function is good, it is the function of the Buddha. From what does the function come? It comes from the self-nature.”

(Translation: The self-nature (the true mind) can contain the ten thousand dharmas, and so is named the storehouse consciousness. If the self-nature gives rise to thinking, that is the turning consciousness, which produces the six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness). The six consciousnesses go out through the six gates (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) and see the six dusts (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas). Thus the eighteen realms (the six consciousnesses, the six gates, and the six dusts) are all the self-nature at work. If the self-nature is perverse, these eighteen realms give rise to eighteen perverse functions; if the self-nature is right, these eighteen realms give rise to eighteen right functions. If the function is evil, it is the function of sentient beings; if good, it is the function of the Buddha. From what does the function come? It comes from the self-nature (the true mind).)

[The true mind’s wondrous essence is originally unmoving, quiet, true, and eternal. When the wondrous function appears upon the true essence, it is no hindrance to follow the stream and attain the wondrous. Therefore the patriarch’s verse says: “The mind follows the ten thousand conditions; where it turns, it is truly profound. Following the stream, one recognizes the nature; without joy and without sorrow
(without love and hate, taking and rejecting)

.” Therefore at all times, in all movement and action, going east and west, eating and dressing, picking up the spoon and handling the chopsticks, looking left and glancing right, it is all the wondrous function of the true mind appearing.]

The wondrous essence of the true mind is originally unmoving, quiet, true, and eternal. When the wondrous function appears upon the true essence, it is no hindrance to follow the stream and attain the wondrous. Therefore the patriarch’s verse says: “The mind follows the ten thousand conditions; where it turns, it is truly profound. Following the stream, one recognizes the nature; without joy and without sorrow (without love and hate, taking and rejecting).” Therefore at all times, in all movement and action, going east and west, eating and dressing, picking up the spoon and handling the chopsticks, looking left and glancing right, it is all the wondrous function of the true mind appearing.
This passage says that if one “follows the stream and recognizes the nature,” then all movement and action is the right function of the true mind when awake.
[The mind follows the ten thousand conditions; where it turns, it is truly profound] Knowing all dharmas without being moved by them. The Vimalakirti Sutra says: “
He well discerns the characteristics of all dharmas
(the characteristics of all dharmas)
yet in the foremost meaning
(the true characteristic of all dharmas)
he does not move.”
The Mahaparinirvana Sutra says

“All dharmas are false; where they cease, that is named the real, that is named the true characteristic, that is named the dharma-realm, named the ultimate wisdom, named the foremost meaning truth, named the foremost meaning emptiness.”

[The foremost meaning truth] The supreme, perfect, and ultimate truth. [Following the stream, one recognizes the nature] As time flows on, one always recognizes the nature of the characteristics of all dharmas that one meets —
“all characteristics are false and delusive”

(the Diamond Sutra). This is “meeting characteristics and returning to the nature”: deluded thoughts are originally still, the dusts of the senses are originally empty; empty and still without darkness, still and illuminating before one. In this way one is not bound and turned by the characteristics of the senses — following the stream, one attains the wondrous.

[Ordinary men are deluded and inverted: when dressing, they take it only as dressing; when eating, they take it only as eating; in all their affairs they merely follow characteristics, and so the true mind is in daily use and they do not notice it, is before their eyes and they do not know it. But one who recognizes the nature does not lose the true mind in movement and action. Therefore the patriarch says: “In the womb it is called the body; in the world it is called a man; in the eye it beholds, in the ear it hears, in the nose it smells fragrance, in the mouth it talks, in the hand it grasps, in the foot it runs. When it manifests everywhere it contains the sand-grain worlds; when it gathers in, it is held within a single mote of dust.... Those who know it take it as the Buddha-nature; those who do not call it the spirit.”]

Ordinary men are deluded and inverted: when dressing they take it only as dressing, when eating they take it only as eating, and all that they do merely follows characteristics (they do not “follow the stream and recognize the nature”); and so the true mind is in daily use and they do not notice it, and is before their eyes and they do not know it. But one who recognizes the nature does not lose the true mind in movement and action. Therefore the patriarch says: “The true mind in the womb is called the body; in the world it is called a man; in the eye it beholds, in the ear it hears, in the nose it distinguishes fragrance, in the tongue it talks, in the hand it grasps, in the foot it runs. When the true mind manifests everywhere, it contains worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges (describing how great the true mind is when it manifests everywhere); when the true mind gathers in, it can be held within a single mote of dust (describing how small the true mind is when it gathers in). Those who know it know this is the Buddha-nature; those who do not call it the spirit.”

[When it manifests everywhere it contains the sand-grain worlds, when it gathers in it is held within a single mote of dust] This speaks of the true mind being able to be great and able to be small. [Sand-grain worlds] Worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The sands of the Ganges are a figure for a number that is very, very many.

[Therefore Daowu danced with his tablet, Shigong drew his bow, Mimo raised his fork, Juzhi held up a finger, the one of Xinzhou struck the ground, and Yunyan showed the lion: none of them was other than revealing this great function. If in daily use one is not deluded, one is naturally free and unobstructed in every direction.]

Therefore Daowu danced with his tablet, Shigong drew his bow, Mimo raised his fork, Juzhi held up a finger, the one of Xinzhou struck the ground, and Yunyan showed the lion: none of them was other than revealing the wondrous function of the true mind. If in daily use one is not deluded and inverted, one is naturally free and unobstructed in every direction.

[Daowu danced with his tablet] A monk asked the monk Daowu: “What is the meaning of the patriarch’s coming from the west?” The master (Daowu) bowed with his slip (bamboo tablet), saying: “Yes.” [Tablet (
hu
)] The bamboo tablet held by ministers at court audiences in ancient times, used for noting matters.
